cards.title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol

depth.text: Brave Search now lets **AI agents** pay per search, with **no account** to set up

Each **unpaid request** gets a 402 Payment Required response with the price and payment details; the agent retries with **signed USDC**, and results come with a receipt. LLM Context and web, news, image, video, and local searches each cost **$0.005 ($5 per 1,000)**; Base gas fees are covered for a limited time.

cards.title: Why Zig over C for Systems Programming

depth.text: someone explains why **Zig** is their pick for **new systems code**, even though **C** still matters

The author says **errdefer** keeps cleanup next to each allocation and runs it only when the function errors; Zig runs those cleanups in reverse order. Its **slices** carry their length, so an out-of-bounds index is caught in debug and safe modes. The trade-off: **C** has more tools, books, people who know it, and compiler support for more chips, and is more stable.

cards.camps: Two camps: Zig fans like its built-in error handling and checks; C advocates say modern tools cover many of the same things and prefer C's stability and ecosystem.

comments.text: Zig is a nice language, but those articles always compare new languages against old-style C without use of modern tools. Most of the listed advantages you can have in C as well if you are willing to adopt modern tooling and style: signed overflow checking: sanitizers, errors you can not ignore: [[nodiscard]], slice type which know their size: variably-modified types or span types. Defer will also…

I’ve settled on a dialect of C++ for systems programming after using C for a long time. It’s mostly C-like and I disable exceptions, RTTI, etc. but I do use templates, overloads, methods, lambdas, etc. I have my own object system with constructor methods that all return a status code so you don’t need exceptions, my own stdlib for containers, buffered I/O, networking, hashing, math, threading…

Also, Zig is as at least as expressive as C++ (but without the implicitness and general language complexity that makes reviewing some sensitive code, where you need to see exactly what operations are performed, hard), and it supports arenas better than C/C++/Rust.
All these new languages are unreadable relative to C. If, like me, you like explicit stuff like for (size_t i = 0; i <= n; i++) total += a[i]; all these new languages won't do it.

cards.title: Relax: JIT compiler for Rust to reduce build times

depth.text: someone built a **Rust compiler** that runs code as it builds and **patches edits into the running program**

Each function is compiled on its first call, and hot ones are optimized while the program runs; function-body edits can be patched without losing state. It’s **experimental**, doesn’t run every crate yet, and its optimized code took **1.12× as long on x64** and **1.24× as long on arm64** as rustc’s release build across 21 workloads.
data: Optimized code time vs rustc release on x64
Optimized code time vs rustc release on arm64

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters report failures, miscompiles, and unusably slow patches; others praise the faster edit-run idea and call the compiler ambitious.

cards.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS

Campaign, local Multiplayer with bots, and local Zombies run at **about 60fps**; the DLC maps require being in your Steam library, heat issues remain, and split-screen is in progress while LAN is planned. glossary.office suite: A set of programs for tasks like writing, spreadsheets and presentations.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.MitM: Man-in-the-middle: a setup where you sit between a device and the internet to watch or change its messages.
glossary.root CA: Certification Authority: the top-level organization a device trusts when deciding whether a website's certificate is valid.
glossary.MQTT: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport: a way for devices and software to pass updates over a network.
glossary.provisioning: Setting a device up with details like which Wi-Fi network it should join.
glossary.Home Assistant integration: A small add-on that lets Home Assistant work with another device.
glossary.HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the rules web browsers and servers use to send web pages and other requests.
glossary.OAuth: A way to let an app access parts of an account without being given the password.
glossary.MCPs: Connections that let Claude use outside apps, such as business software.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.health check: An automatic test that checks whether a server is working.
glossary.SLA: Service-level agreement: a provider's promise about how reliably its service will work.
glossary.single point of failure: One component whose breakdown can stop the whole service from working.
glossary.extrapolation: Using a trend in past data to guess what might happen next.
glossary.window manager: The part of a graphical desktop that controls how app windows are placed, moved, and switched.
glossary.X Window System: A system that lets programs display graphical windows and respond to keyboard and mouse input.
glossary.RandR: A part of the X display system used to handle screen settings, including multiple monitors.
glossary.Xinerama: A way for a desktop to spread one large screen across multiple monitors.
glossary.2FA: Two-factor authentication: a sign-in check that asks for a second proof of identity as well as a password.
glossary.MX: Mail Exchange: a setting that tells other email services where to deliver email for a domain.
glossary.SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the system mail apps use to send messages.
glossary.failover: A backup system taking over automatically when the main one stops working.
glossary.network capacity upgrade: Work to give a network more room to handle activity.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.ghostwriter: Someone paid to write for another person, often without being credited.
glossary.provenance: The record of where an artwork came from and who owned it.
glossary.REPL loop: Read–eval–print loop: a cycle where you enter something, see the result, and try again.
glossary.RL loop: Reinforcement learning loop: a try-and-check cycle where each result helps decide what to try next.
glossary.NP-Complete: A label for problems where checking a proposed answer can be straightforward, but finding one may require an enormous search.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.x402 protocol: An open payment method that lets an agent attach payment to a web request instead of logging in with an API key.
glossary.HTTP 402 Payment Required: A web server's way of saying a request needs payment before it will run.

glossary.CLI wallet: A wallet you use by typing commands into a text prompt instead of clicking through an app.
glossary.gas fees: Charges for processing a transaction on a blockchain.
glossary.errdefer: A Zig instruction that runs cleanup code only if the function returns an error.
glossary.slice: A piece of data that keeps track of how long it is, so code can check where it ends.
glossary.C ABI: Application Binary Interface: agreed rules that let code written in different languages call each other's functions.
glossary.undefined behavior: A situation where C++ gives no guarantee about what the program will do.
glossary.sanitizer: A checking tool that can catch certain mistakes while a program runs.
glossary.provider-agnostic: Able to work with services from different companies, so you can switch if one goes down.
glossary.code agent: An AI tool that can take on programming tasks, like changing code or fixing problems.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.quota: The amount of usage a service allows before it limits what you can do.
glossary.open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
glossary.on-premise: Software or equipment run on a company's own computers rather than rented online services.
glossary.webhook: A message one service sends another when something happens.
glossary.OTP: One-time password: a code meant to work for one login or for a short time.
glossary.theorem: A mathematical statement shown to be true through reasoning.
glossary.Gabelsberger shorthand: A German shorthand system Gödel used to write notes quickly.
glossary.proof assistant: Software that checks whether a mathematical proof follows its rules.
glossary.incompleteness theorems: Gödel’s result that some true mathematical statements cannot be proved or disproved inside the system they belong to.
glossary.JIT: Just-in-time compilation: compiling a program as it runs, rather than beforehand.
glossary.hot patching: Changing code in a program that is already running, without restarting it.
glossary.borrow checker: The Rust tool that checks code won’t use a value after it’s gone or let it be changed unsafely.
glossary.incremental build: A rebuild that reuses unchanged work and only handles what changed.
glossary.crate: A reusable package of Rust code that you can add to a project.
glossary.PPI: Producer Price Index: a measure of how prices change for things producers sell.
glossary.YoY: Year over year: comparing a figure with the same period one year earlier.
glossary.budget deficit: When a government spends more money than it brings in.
glossary.quantitative easing: When a central bank buys financial assets to add money to the economy.
glossary.USD: United States dollar: the currency used in the United States.
glossary.Rome Statute: The agreement that created the International Criminal Court and sets out what it can do.
glossary.States Parties: Countries that have joined the Rome Statute.
glossary.complementarity: The rule that lets the Court step in when a country will not or cannot investigate and prosecute a case itself.
glossary.blocking mechanism: An EU law that tells European parties to ignore US sanctions and keep supplying the Court and its staff.
glossary.BitTorrent: A way to share a file by downloading pieces from other people's copies, rather than one central server.
glossary.tracker: A service that helps people sharing a file find one another.
glossary.seed: The starting number that helps determine what numbers a random-number generator produces.
glossary.static recompilation: Translating a game's existing code into code for a different system before running it.
glossary.AOT: Ahead-of-time compilation: turning a program into an executable before it runs.
glossary.ARM64: A type of chip design that software can be built for so it runs directly on matching computers.
glossary.emulator: A program that imitates another service so you can try your software without using the real one.
glossary.x86 interpreter: A helper program that handles instructions meant for another kind of computer when the main conversion misses them.
glossary.DLC: Downloadable content: extra game content added after the main game.
glossary.LAN: Local Area Network: devices connected to the same nearby network.
glossary.Wine: Software that lets Windows programs run on other operating systems.
glossary.Cargo: Rust’s tool for building Rust projects.
glossary.minimum-publish-age: A rule that makes Cargo wait a set amount of time after a package version appears before using it.
glossary.dependency cooldowns: A way to wait before using newly published package versions, giving problems time to be spotted.
glossary.never type: A type for code that never reaches a normal result because it exits or keeps running instead.
glossary.supply-chain attack: An attack that slips harmful code into software people get through a tool or package they trust.
glossary.digitizing: Turning artwork into instructions for an embroidery machine, including how the stitches should go.
glossary.PES/DST: File types used to store embroidery designs so machines can read them.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.ITAR: International Traffic in Arms Regulations: US rules that restrict sharing certain military-related technology.
glossary.fiduciary duty: A legal responsibility to make decisions in the interests of a company or the people it represents.
glossary.interim CEO: A temporary chief executive who runs a company until a longer-term choice is made.
glossary.model router: A tool that picks which AI model handles a task.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.long-horizon task: A job that takes many steps or keeps running over a longer period.
glossary.dwarf planet: A nearly round object orbiting a star that hasn't cleared similar-sized debris from its path.
glossary.infrared light: Light we can't see that lets astronomers measure heat coming from an object.
glossary.photographic plates: Flat sheets used to record photographs before modern digital cameras.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.SM: Streaming Multiprocessor: one of a GPU’s processing units that handles calculations.
glossary.hardware fingerprint: A pattern in a model’s starting numbers that can hint at which chip created them.
glossary.distillation: Training a smaller AI to imitate the answers of a larger one.
glossary.export controls: Rules that limit where a company can sell certain goods, often for security reasons.
glossary.TRT: Testosterone replacement therapy: medical treatment that provides testosterone to someone whose body has too little.
glossary.abstractions: Simpler ways to organize code so you can work with an idea without handling every detail.
glossary.IPC: Inter-process communication: a way for separate programs on one computer to exchange information.
glossary.L3 cache: A processor's shared stash of data, meant to save trips to main memory.
glossary.SMT: Simultaneous multithreading: a way for one processor core to work on more than one stream of instructions at a time.
glossary.VNNI: Vector Neural Network Instructions: special processor commands used for number-heavy tasks such as the AI and video work mentioned here.
glossary.parameters: Learned values inside a model that shape the answers it gives.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.tokens/s: Tokens per second: a rough measure of how quickly a model produces text.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.server models: AI models that run on a provider's computers rather than directly on your device.
glossary.Swift API: A way for an app written in Swift to use features from another piece of software.
glossary.Dynamic Profiles: Different saved setups an app can switch between, each choosing its AI model, available tools, and instructions.
glossary.Evaluations framework: A way to test whether an AI feature still works when the request or setup changes.
glossary.wholesale electricity prices: The prices utilities pay for electricity before it is delivered to homes.
glossary.energy burden: How much of a household's income goes to paying for energy.
glossary.baseload generation: Power supply meant to run steadily, rather than only when demand peaks.
glossary.transmission infrastructure: The lines and equipment that carry electricity from where it is made to where it is used.
glossary.type confusion: When a program treats data as one kind of thing even though it was created as another.
glossary.composite type: A database value made up of named fields, like a row with several columns.
glossary.prepared statement: A query the database works out first and can run later with values supplied separately.
glossary.bytea: PostgreSQL’s type for storing bytes that aren’t necessarily readable text.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.Datum: A PostgreSQL container for a value, which may hold the value itself or refer to where it is stored.
glossary.letter rogatory: A formal request asking another country’s authorities to help gather evidence in a legal case.
glossary.subpoena: A legal order telling someone to provide records or appear in court.
glossary.data centers: Large buildings full of computers that store or process information.
glossary.AUv3: Audio Unit version 3: Apple's way for music-making add-ons to run inside compatible apps.
glossary.VST: Virtual Studio Technology: a format for add-ons that give music software new instruments or effects.
glossary.MIDI: Musical Instrument Digital Interface: a way for music software and instruments to share notes and timing.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
